item.title: Gioele La Manno
item.description:
Bio

I earned my PhD at Karolinska Instituet and I am proud alumnus of the Linnarsson Lab. My original training is in Biotechnology (BSc @UNIPA) and Biomedicine (MSc @KI) but nowadays I will probably turn around if somebody is calling out for a Molecular Biologist, Computational Biologist or Bioinformatician.

My research focuses on understanding brain development. I am particularly interested in describing the sequence of states that embryonic stem cells go through during their differentiation towards mature neurons.

I have been tackling this question using machine learning tools on the wealth of data provided by single cell RNA sequencing, a technique I have been working with and developing since its early times.

My long-term goal is to contribute in making biology from a descriptive to a predictive science.

item.title: Gioele named a Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher 2026
item.description:
Gioele La Manno has been named a Clarivate Highly Cited Researcher in the Cross-Field category for 2026, his third consecutive inclusion following 2024 and 2025. His primary affiliation on the list is EPFL.

Announced on 18 November, this year’s list recognises 6,802 researchers across more than 1,200 institutions in 62 countries and regions. Clarivate awarded 7,090 recognitions, including 3,251 in the Cross-Field category. The distinction between researchers and recognitions matters: some people appear in more than one subject category. Switzerland accounts for 151 recognitions, placing it eighth worldwide and representing 2.1% of the total.

Selection draws on papers that rank among the most cited 1% for their field and publication year over an eleven-year period. Citation data are assessed alongside expert review and checks on publication and citation patterns. The result recognises sustained influence on subsequent research, rather than the reception of a single recent paper.

For Gioele, the Cross-Field category is a fitting reflection of a research path that connects neuroscience, molecular biology and computational methods. His work asks how the brain’s cellular diversity emerges, while developing ways to measure and interpret that diversity. Contributions range from mapping developing brain cell types and introducing RNA velocity to investigating the spatial organisation of lipids in the brain. These approaches give other researchers tools and reference maps for asking their own biological questions.

At 36, Gioele has now received this recognition three years in a row. When he first appeared on the list in 2024, EPFL described him, then aged 34, as one of the youngest researchers on the list. He is potentially the youngest researcher with a primary Swiss affiliation on the 2026 list, although an exact age ranking has not been established. The recognition marks an early milestone in a research programme that continues to grow at EPFL.

For the lab, the significance of the Cross-Field recognition lies in how these contributions travel between disciplines. A computational method developed to investigate brain development can help researchers studying other tissues; a reference atlas can provide a starting point for experiments far beyond the questions that motivated its creation. Making methods, code and data available allows those connections to develop and gives the work a life beyond the original publication.

This third inclusion accompanies a year in which the lab and its collaborators published the Lipid Brain Atlas, extending the study of brain diversity beyond genes and cell types to its molecular composition. It reflects the lab’s continuing interest in bringing complementary measurements together to understand how the brain develops and functions.

Behind the individual name on the list is a collective effort: students, colleagues, mentors and collaborators who have developed methods, generated data and shared ideas. We are grateful to everyone who has contributed, and to the researchers who continue to use and build on this work.

Read the 2026 announcement or explore the official Clarivate Highly Cited Researchers page.

item.title: Celebrating the Eppendorf & Science Prize in Washington
item.description:
On 15 November 2026, Gioele received the Eppendorf & Science Prize for Neurobiology at the award ceremony in Washington, D.C., during the week of the Society for Neuroscience meeting.

The celebration brought together experts in neuroscience, editors from Science, and representatives of Eppendorf. Among those present were Marina Picciotto, Mattia Maroso, Senior Editor at Science and chair of the prize jury, and Axel Jahns of Eppendorf. It was a special opportunity to share the lab’s work and celebrate with the wider neuroscience community.

The prize recognises Gioele’s work on the molecular organisation of brain lipids, including the Lipid Brain Atlas, developed in collaboration with Giovanni D’Angelo’s group. Thank you to everyone in the lab and to our collaborators whose contributions made this achievement possible.

Read the official Eppendorf announcement and our original prize announcement.

item.title: Congratulations, PI Toni! A new lab in Granada
item.description:
Congratulations to Antonio Herrera Camacho on becoming a Principal Investigator at the University of Granada! Supported by a Ramón y Cajal fellowship, Toni is starting his own independent research group. We are proud to celebrate this milestone with him.

Since joining the La Manno Lab in 2021, Toni has brought his experience in developmental biology to our efforts to understand how the brain forms. His work combined embryo culture, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell analysis, with a particular interest in how folate deficiency affects brain development. Alongside his research, he helped students learn experimental approaches and develop their own projects.

His contributions also span several of the lab’s collaborative publications, including uMAIA, Spotiflow, and VeloCycle, all published in Nature Methods.

Seeing a colleague take the step to leading an independent lab is a special moment for our team. We look forward to the questions Toni and his new group will explore, and to continuing our scientific collaborations.

Thank you, Toni, for five years of science, mentorship, and friendship. We will miss having you in the lab, but there is much to celebrate. All the best for your new lab in Granada, PI Toni!

item.title: Gioele wins the Eppendorf & Science Prize for Neurobiology
item.description:
We are delighted to celebrate Gioele La Manno’s 2026 Eppendorf & Science Prize for Neurobiology.

The prize recognises research on brain lipid diversity, including the Lipid Brain Atlas. This milestone reflects a sustained collaboration across the lab and with Giovanni D’Angelo’s group.

Read Gioele’s accompanying essay, “Fats that think?”, in Science, and the official Eppendorf announcement.

Thank you to the students, researchers, and collaborators whose work made this possible.

item.title: Thank you and farewell, Francesco!
item.description:
We say goodbye to Francesco Danese and thank him for his time in the La Manno Lab.

Francesco joined us in August 2025 from Sapienza University of Rome for his master’s thesis.

Working with Luca Fusar Bassini, Francesco contributed to our neuroscience knowledge graph project, helping turn information from the scientific literature into structured knowledge that can support biological research. His work brought together machine learning, data science, and the practical challenges of processing a large collection of scientific papers.

Thank you, Francesco, for your contribution and collaboration. We wish you all the best for what comes next and look forward to staying in touch!
